ruling_applied: STANDING OWNER RULING 2026-09-20: default REPRODUCE; CONSEQUENTIAL (C1..C6) defects are neither reproduced nor fixed, they are isolated and escalated individually.

triaged.one_line: applyConfigOptions clears effortConfigID and fastConfigID on every call but not modeConfigID or modelConfigID, so a set_config_option reply that omits thought_level or the fast model_config permanently drops the effort slider and Fast toggle for the session.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED verbatim. ACPSession.swift:327 'private func applyConfigOptions(_ options: [JSONValue])'; :330 'effortConfigID = nil'; :331 'fastConfigID = nil'. No corresponding reset of modeConfigID or modelConfigID exists: they are only ever assigned, at :338 ('modelConfigID = id') and :364 ('modeConfigID = id'). :372 'effortConfigID = id' and :377 'fastConfigID = id' are the only re-arm sites. setConfigOption at :484 does 'if let options = result?[configOptions]?.array { applyConfigOptions(options) }', so the app's own session/set_config_option reply re-enters the function. The consumers are :456 'if let effort, !effort.isEmpty, let effortConfigID, effort != currentEffort' and :460 'if let fastConfigID', both of which stop firing once the ids are nil. Every line number in the register is exact.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: After switching model in a chat on an ACP provider (Cursor, OpenCode, Grok, Devin) whose reply advertises a configOptions array without a thought_level/effort entry or without the fast model_config, the effort slider and the Fast toggle stop being sent for the rest of that session. The user can still move the slider in the UI; the value is simply never transmitted, so turns silently run at the agent's own default. Recovered by anything that restarts the session (closing and reopening the chat, changing a launch-signature field). No data is lost and nothing is written anywhere.
triaged.notes: Dropped UI affordance plus a misleading control, explicitly named in the ordinary-quirk list. Reproduce the asymmetry exactly: nil only effortConfigID and fastConfigID at the top of the function.

triaged.one_line: AntigravitySession stores runtimeMode and interactionMode in init and on every send but never reads them; start() builds its flags from configuration.* instead.
triaged.verified_against_source: PARTIALLY WRONG - the dead-store fact is right, the stated consequence is not. Source facts: 'private var runtimeMode: RuntimeMode' :23 and 'private var interactionMode: InteractionMode' :24; assigned :57-58 in init and :150-151 in send(_:); the only reads in the file are the PARAMETERS of modeArguments at :123/:128/:135, and the one call site at :88 passes 'configuration.runtimeMode' and 'configuration.interactionMode', not the stored fields. A grep for runtimeMode and interactionMode returns exactly lines 23, 24, 57, 58, 88, 123, 128, 135, 150, 151. So both properties are genuinely write-only. CORRECTION to the register's harm claim: 'A mid-thread mode or Plan/Build change cannot reach agy at all, and even a relaunch uses the original modes' is FALSE. ThreadRuntime.swift:504-519 defines SessionSignature with launchRuntimeMode and launchInteraction, and :1414/:1418 populate both from thread.* specifically for .antigravity. :1422 'if let session, session.isRunning, sessionSignature == signature { return session }' therefore fails on any mode or Plan/Build change, and :1496-1523 makeSession builds a brand-new SessionConfiguration from the current thread.runtimeMode / thread.interactionMode and constructs a brand-new AntigravitySession. A tree-wide grep for 'AntigravitySession(' gives exactly one construction site (ThreadRuntime.swift:1516), and start() is only ever called on a freshly made object (ThreadRuntime.swift:1478, :1486, :1547, :1563). A mode change does reach agy, by restart. The same applies to launchModel/launchEffort, so the 'picks up the UPDATED model/effort' asymmetry the register describes does not occur either.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: None that a user can observe. The two properties are dead stores: nothing reads them after assignment, and the restart-on-signature-change path already carries the current modes into the new process. The realistic outcome is only that a reader of the code is misled into thinking per-turn mode state is applied in-session.
triaged.notes: Dead code with zero behavioral effect. I checked the C3/C5 reading deliberately, because runtimeMode gates --dangerously-skip-permissions (AntigravitySession.swift:135-137): if a user tightened permissions mid-thread and the change were dropped, that would be a security-control failure. It is not dropped - the signature forces a relaunch - so C3/C5 do not apply. The port must keep the signature fields for Antigravity (launchRuntimeMode, launchModel, launchEffort, launchInteraction); they are what makes this harmless.

triaged.one_line: The fallback quota percent branch has no lower clamp, so a negative usedRequests yields a negative percent on the usage bar.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED verbatim. CopilotSession.swift:456 reads 'let percent = remaining.map { max(0, min(100, 100 - $0)) } ?? min(100, used / entitlement * 100)'. The primary branch clamps both ends; the fallback clamps only the top. 'used' comes from :455 'snapshot[usedRequests]?.double ?? 0', and 'entitlement > 0' is already guaranteed by the guard at :453, so division is safe but sign is not. The value goes straight into PlanLimits.Window(percent:) at :457-462.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: If GitHub's account.getQuota ever reports a negative usedRequests for a snapshot that also omits remainingPercentage, the Copilot usage bar renders from a negative percent: most likely an empty or visually clipped bar and a nonsense number in the usage panel. Nothing is written, nothing is sent, no turn is affected. Requires the upstream API to return a value it has no reason to return.
triaged.notes: Cosmetic display defect on an implausible input. Reproduce the exact expression, including the asymmetric clamping.

triaged.one_line: refreshCredits has neither the 25-second watchdog nor the defer that refreshPlanLimits uses, and has no forced-read queue, so a hung read leaves the spinner on forever and a concurrent force:true is dropped.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED, both halves, with exact lines. refreshCredits :621-640: 'loadingCredits.insert(provider)' at :632, then 'Task { let balance = await CreditsReader.read(...); loadingCredits.remove(provider); ... }' at :633-639 - the removal is a plain statement after the await, not a defer, and there is no watchdog Task. Compare refreshPlanLimits: :556 insert, :557 'let watchdog = Task { try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(25)); loadingLimits.remove(provider); drainedForcedRead(provider) }', :559 'defer { watchdog.cancel(); loadingLimits.remove(provider); drainedForcedRead(provider) }', and the same pair again at :568/:569/:571 for the non-API-key path. Forced-read queue: :548 'guard !loadingLimits.contains(provider) else { if force { forcedLimitReads.insert(provider) }; return }' with drainedForcedRead at :584-587; refreshCredits :622 is 'guard CreditsReader.exposesCredits(provider), !loadingCredits.contains(provider) else { return }' with no such capture. Every cited line is exact.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: A CreditsReader.read that never returns (a hung HTTPS request to the DeepSeek or Command Code balance endpoint) leaves loadingCredits containing that provider for the rest of the app run: the balance spinner in the usage panel and settings spins forever and no later refresh, forced or not, can get through the :622 guard. The user must restart the app to see a balance again. Separately, a force:true arriving while any read is in flight is discarded, so a 'refresh now' can appear to do nothing. Nothing is written or lost.
triaged.notes: Stuck spinner and a dropped refresh - both named explicitly in the ordinary-quirk list. Reproduce the missing watchdog, the missing defer and the missing forced-read queue; do not quietly add any of the three by copying the refreshPlanLimits shape.

triaged.one_line: The empty-API-key early return clears credits but not creditsFetchedAt, so the stale timestamp makes the 60-second gate suppress the next read.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED verbatim. :627-630 'guard !apiKey.isEmpty else { credits[provider] = nil; return }' - it sets credits to nil and returns, leaving creditsFetchedAt[provider] untouched. The gate is the very next line, :631 'if !force, let fetched = creditsFetchedAt[provider], Date.now.timeIntervalSince(fetched) < 60 { return }'. Both cited line ranges are exact. Reachability check: credits are exposed for exactly two providers (ProviderCredits.swift:58 'provider == .deepseek || provider == .commandcode'). DeepSeek escapes the symptom because ProviderRegistry.swift:394 calls 'refreshCredits(.deepseek, force: true)' after a key validates. Command Code does not: its key is the CLI's own login (:624-625 'CommandCodeAPI.apiKey(environment:)'), it falls into the bare else at :419-421 of the validation switch with no forced read, and its only refresh call sites (SettingsView.swift:762, UsagePanel.swift:73/:76) all pass force defaulted to false. So the described symptom is real and Command Code is where it lands.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: A user who signs commandcode in via its CLI within a minute of the app having observed no key sees a blank Command Code balance in the usage panel and settings for the remainder of that 60-second window, with no explanation. It clears itself. Nothing is written, sent or lost.
triaged.notes: Stale-timestamp quirk, self-healing within a minute. Reproduce the early return exactly as written, without clearing creditsFetchedAt.

triaged.one_line: handshake() throws when the initialize response has no commands array, which also destroys the Claude model catalog even though loadClaudeCatalog only wants .models, and try? swallows the cause.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED verbatim. ClaudeSession.swift:203-205: 'guard let response = message[response]?[response], let commands = response[commands]?.array else { throw ProviderError.failed("Claude could not load its commands.") }', with the success return at :206 'return (models(in: response), SlashCommand.claudeCommands(commands))'. The models are parsed from the same response object and do not depend on commands at all, so the guard couples them. ProviderRegistry.swift:501-505 'private func loadClaudeCatalog(...) async -> [ModelOption]? { ... return try? await ClaudeSession.handshake(executable:directory:environment:).models }' - the try? discards the thrown message and yields nil, and the catalog read only ever wanted .models. Both line ranges are exact, and the error string matches character for character including the full stop.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: A Claude CLI build whose initialize response omits commands leaves the model picker for Claude empty for the run, with no error surfaced anywhere: the user sees no models to choose from and is told nothing about why. Threads still run on whatever model is already stored. Nothing is lost or written.
triaged.notes: Missing affordance plus a swallowed cause. Reproduce both the coupling in the guard and the try? at the catalog call site, including the exact user-facing string 'Claude could not load its commands.'

triaged.one_line: A guard that re-checks two conditions already guaranteed upstream, with nothing able to invalidate them in between: dead, not a safety net.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED verbatim. :567 is 'guard PlanLimitsReader.exposesLimits(provider), !loadingLimits.contains(provider) else { return }'. Both conditions are established at :547 'guard PlanLimitsReader.exposesLimits(provider) else { return }' and :548 'guard !loadingLimits.contains(provider) else { ... return }'. I checked the code between :548 and :567 for anything that could invalidate them: :549 is a pure read of limitsFetchedAt, :550-565 is the 'if provider.isAPIKeyBased { ... return }' block which returns on every path it takes, and there is no await and no mutation of loadingLimits reachable on the fall-through. exposesLimits is a pure static function. The guard can never fire.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: Nothing. Dead condition, invisible to any user.
triaged.notes: Redundant guard - explicitly listed as ordinary. Carry it across so the two functions stay line-comparable with upstream.

triaged.one_line: PiCLI hard-codes the support-directory literal 'Droppy Code/pi' while CommandCodeAPI and MCPBridgeSource interpolate AppInfo.name, so a build with a different display name scatters helper files across two roots.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED. PiCLI.swift:13-18 'static var supportDirectory: URL { let base = ...; return base.appendingPathComponent("Droppy Code/pi", isDirectory: true) }' - the literal is on :17. CommandCodeAPI.swift:440-445 uses 'base.appendingPathComponent("(AppInfo.name)/CommandCode", isDirectory: true)' at :443, with AppInfo.name interpolated. MCPBridgeSource.swift:240-245 uses 'base.appendingPathComponent("(AppInfo.name)/MCP", isDirectory: true)' at :243, likewise interpolated. All three cited sites are exact.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: On a build whose display name is not 'Droppy Code', Pi's gate extension and per-session gate files live under a differently named Application Support folder from Command Code's mod and the MCP bridge. Nothing breaks: each subsystem writes and reads through its own accessor, so all three are internally consistent. The outcome is untidy on-disk layout and a stale product name in a path. No data loss, no functional failure.
triaged.notes: Inconsistent naming - explicitly listed as ordinary. Flagged as a port decision rather than a behavior to copy blindly: the Windows port has a different product name, so the literal must be resolved deliberately and the choice recorded in the adaptation register. The inconsistency itself is not consequential.

triaged.one_line: A port repick after the listener fails leaves every provider config written this launch pointing at the dead port, because nothing in the repick path re-runs MCPProviderConfig.writeAll.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED. MCPProxy.swift:118-131 is the '.failed(let error)' branch: it prints, cancels the listener, clears self.listener, and 'if canRepick { self.listen(on: Self.repickPort(), canRepick: false) }' at :126-127. repickPort (:26-32) mutates portBox and rewrites the port file but notifies nobody. MCPStore.swift:22-28 'init() { load(); MCPProxy.shared.start(); exportAll() }' - exportAll is called synchronously at :27, immediately after start(), whereas a listener .failed state is delivered asynchronously on the proxy's queue. A tree-wide grep for writeAll returns the definition at MCPProviderConfig.swift:148 and exactly one call site, MCPStore.swift:286 inside exportAll. exportAll's other callers are MCPStore.swift:133, :148, :187 and :343 - connect, disconnect, setEnabled and probe-success - none of which the repick triggers. Every cited line is exact.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: On a launch where the saved port cannot be bound (a second copy of the app, or a Dev build over a mirrored library), every provider config file written during that launch names the dead port. Agents started in that session get connection-refused on loopback for OAuth MCP servers, so those servers' tools are simply unavailable, until the user does something that re-runs exportAll (connect, disconnect, enable/disable a server) or restarts. Failure is loud and local: refused TCP connections to 127.0.0.1, no traffic to any other destination, nothing written incorrectly beyond a stale port number in config files that the next exportAll overwrites.
triaged.notes: I checked C6 specifically: the stale value is a loopback port number, so a wrong port can only reach 127.0.0.1 and in practice reaches nothing. No data goes anywhere the user did not choose. Degraded MCP availability with a user-reachable workaround.

triaged.one_line: The SSE relay emits one chunked-transfer chunk per byte, each an awaited NWConnection.send.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED verbatim. MCPProxy.swift:387-392 inside writeBack (:369): 'for try await byte in stream { var frame = Data("1CRLF".utf8); frame.append(byte); frame.append(Data("CRLF".utf8)); await send(connection, frame) }' where CRLF is the literal carriage-return line-feed escape. Each iteration builds a 6-byte-overhead frame around a single payload byte and awaits the send. The terminator 'await send(connection, Data("0CRLFCRLF".utf8))' follows at :395.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: Streaming MCP tool results through the proxy are slow and CPU-hungry: seven bytes on the wire per payload byte and one async round trip each. A large streamed result feels sluggish and burns loopback throughput. The data that arrives is correct - chunked transfer encoding reassembles identically - so nothing is corrupted or lost.
triaged.notes: Slow behavior with correct output - explicitly listed as ordinary. Reproduce the per-byte framing exactly, including the one-hex-digit chunk header and the zero-length terminator.

triaged.one_line: The non-SSE path accumulates the entire upstream body one byte at a time before sending anything, so there is no streaming and an O(n) per-byte await.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED verbatim, with a one-line adjustment to the range. MCPProxy.swift:399 'var payload = Data()', :400-402 'for try await byte in stream { payload.append(byte) }', :403 appends the Content-Length header from payload.count, then the head and the whole payload go out in a single await send at :407. The register cites :398-402; the loop and its setup are :399-402. Behavior as described.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: A large non-streaming tool result is held entirely in memory and assembled one byte per await before the client sees anything: noticeable latency before the first byte and a memory spike proportional to the result size. Output is byte-correct. No loss, no corruption.
triaged.notes: Slow and memory-hungry but correct. Reproduce the buffer-then-send shape, including the accurate Content-Length it makes possible.

triaged.one_line: A request that ends early below its declared Content-Length has its truncated body relayed upstream with no error.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED. readBody is :260-281. The completion path is :276-277: 'else if isComplete || error != nil { self.routeRequest(connection: connection, method: method, path: path, clientHeaders: clientHeaders, body: next) }' - next is whatever arrived, shorter than need, and routeRequest relays it. The refusals do sit elsewhere and do not cover this: 413 at :250 for an oversized body, and the 400/411 checks live earlier in the header parse. The register's cited range is one line long at the end; the substance is exact.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: If the local MCP client dies or the loopback connection breaks mid-body, the proxy forwards a truncated JSON-RPC payload to the remote MCP server instead of abandoning the request. JSON truncation is essentially always invalid JSON, so the server answers a parse error, which the proxy then tries to write back to a connection that is already gone. The practical effect is one junk request in a remote server's log. The truncated payload is a prefix of a request the user's own client had already composed and was already sending to that same chosen server, so nothing new is disclosed and no new destination is contacted.
triaged.notes: I considered C4 and C6 and rejected both. C4: nothing of the user's is stored or overwritten; the request simply fails upstream and the failure is visible as an error, not silent. C6: the destination is the same upstream the user connected that server to, unchanged. Reproduce the early-completion relay exactly.

triaged.one_line: WWW-Authenticate is not copied back, so a 401 from an OAuth upstream reaches the client bare and RFC 9728 discovery through a proxy route cannot work.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED. writeBack at :369 assembles its headers array from exactly three upstream fields: Content-Type (:370-373), Mcp-Session-Id (:375-377) and Cache-Control (:378-380). A grep for WWW-Authenticate in MCPProxy.swift returns nothing. The status code itself is preserved (:384 and :406 pass response.statusCode to statusHead), so the client sees a 401 with no challenge and no resource-metadata pointer.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: A client that would discover an OAuth authorization server from the 401 challenge cannot do so through a proxy route, so that discovery-driven sign-in path just does not work and the server shows as failing. Note the direction of the effect: the proxy withholds an authentication hint, it does not bypass or relax any check. Droppy's own sign-in does not depend on this - MCPOAuth performs discovery and attaches the Bearer token itself at MCPProxy.swift:341-350.
triaged.notes: I checked C3 explicitly. Dropping WWW-Authenticate does not weaken authentication: the upstream still rejects, the 401 still propagates, and the proxy still fails closed. It removes a capability, it does not remove a control. Reproduce the three-header allowlist exactly.

triaged.one_line: The bridge never kills a spawned child: a server hanging in initialize or tools/list is abandoned after CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS = 15000 and its process lives for the whole lifetime of the Pi / Command Code host.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED. 'const CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS = 15000;' at :17. withTimeout (:50-56) races the connect promise against a setTimeout that rejects with new Error('timed out') and only clears the timer in .finally - it has no handle on the child and no way to signal it. connectStdio (:76 onward) spawns at :80-83 with stdio ['pipe','pipe','ignore'] and installs child.on('error', fail) and child.on('exit', ...), but a grep of the whole file for kill, SIGTERM and unref returns nothing at all. loadMCPTools (:218-233) catches and logs console.error with the exact text 'droppy mcp: skipping ' + server + ': ' + errorText(error) at :230 and moves on, leaving the child running. Every cited element matches, including the log string character for character.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: Each Pi or Command Code run that meets a hung or slow MCP server leaves that server's process running for the life of the host process, holding whatever the server holds. Across a long session with a repeatedly hung server this accumulates orphan processes and their memory. No user data is touched, nothing is deleted, and the processes die with the host. On Windows the same leak additionally risks orphan processes keeping file handles open in the project folder - a port hazard worth noting, not a change in classification.
triaged.notes: Resource leak with no lasting harm to the user's data or state. Reproduce the absence of a kill path and the exact timeout value and log string.

triaged.one_line: loadMCPTools connects servers strictly sequentially with await inside the loop, so N hung servers cost N * 15 seconds of startup.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED verbatim. :220-232 'for (const server of Object.keys(servers)) { ... tools.push(...await withTimeout(connectRemote(server, entry))); ... tools.push(...await withTimeout(connectStdio(server, entry))); ... }'. Both awaits are inside the loop body, there is no Promise.all and no concurrency, and each hung server burns the full CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS = 15000 before the next is tried.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: With, say, four unreachable MCP servers configured, a Pi or Command Code run stalls a full minute before the agent has any tools. Purely a delay; the tool list that eventually arrives is correct.
triaged.notes: Slow startup - explicitly listed as ordinary. Reproduce the sequential loop; do not parallelize it.

triaged.one_line: On probe success, states[id] = .connected is written unconditionally while connectedAt/serverVersion/tools are written only if a connection row exists, so a card can show connected with a tool count while nothing is persisted and no provider gets the server.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED verbatim. MCPStore.swift:335-340 'if var connection = connections[entry.id] { connection.connectedAt = .now; connection.serverVersion = result.serverVersion; connection.tools = result.tools; connections[entry.id] = connection }', then :341 'states[entry.id] = .connected(toolCount: result.tools.count)' outside that if, then :342 save() and :343 exportAll(). The downstream filter is :41-44 'connections.values.filter { $0.isEnabled && $0.connectedAt != nil }', so with no row the server is absent from enabledServers and therefore from every provider config and from the proxy's route table. The register's reachability claim via refresh(_:) is supportable: refresh (:136-141) calls startProbe without requiring a row, and disconnect (:120-134) removes the row at :130 while cancelling the probe at :121 - so the window is a refresh issued against an entry whose row is gone. Narrow but real.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: The MCP settings card for that server reads 'connected' with a tool count while the server is in fact wired up to nothing: no agent can use it, nothing was saved, and the state vanishes on the next launch. The user is misinformed about one server's status and may wonder why its tools never appear. No data is lost or written incorrectly.
triaged.notes: Misleading UI state - explicitly listed as ordinary. Reproduce the unconditional state write outside the row check.

triaged.one_line: Variable uses the synthesized decoder, so a stored variable object missing isSecret throws keyNotFound, the throw escapes decodeIfPresent, and the outer try? silently drops every custom server.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED, and the consequence is worse than the entry states. MCPCustom.swift:15-19 'struct Variable: Codable, Sendable, Hashable, Identifiable { var key: String; var isSecret = false; var id: String { key } }' - no custom init(from:), so Swift synthesizes one, and a synthesized Decodable initializer does not fall back to a property's default value for a missing key: it calls decode(Bool.self, forKey: .isSecret) and throws keyNotFound. MCPCustomServer's own hand-written init(from:) at :38-48 is tolerant for its own keys (:42-47 all decodeIfPresent) but 'env = try container.decodeIfPresent([Variable].self, forKey: .env) ?? []' at :45 propagates any error thrown from inside the array's element decoding - decodeIfPresent only absorbs a missing key, never a malformed value. The outer catch is MCPStore.swift:245-248 'if let data = try? Data(contentsOf: MCPPaths.customsURL), let list = try? JSONDecoder().decode([MCPCustomServer].self, from: data) { customs = list }' - one bad element discards the whole array. The doc comment promising tolerance is :36-37 (the register says :37-38), and it is contradicted for exactly this case. ADDITION the register does not record: the drop is not read-only. customs stays empty, and the next saveCustom (:155-188, saveCustoms at :175) or deleteCustom (:191-197, saveCustoms at :196) writes the now-empty array back over MCPPaths.customsURL via 'try? data.write(to: MCPPaths.customsURL, options: .atomic)' (:275). The user's definitions are then gone from disk with no backup and no message.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: A user with a hand-edited or partially corrupted mcp-customs.json - the exact case the file's own doc comment says is tolerated - opens the app and finds Settings > MCP > Custom empty, with no error anywhere. If they then add a replacement server, saveCustoms atomically overwrites the file with the single new entry, and every previous custom server definition (name, command, args, url, variable keys) is permanently gone. Keychain secrets are not destroyed on this path - deleteCustom is never called - so they survive as orphans, which bounds the damage: this is lost configuration, retypeable, not lost credentials and not lost project work. Probability is low: isSecret has been present since the file's first commit (75e30f217, 2026-09-18), so no shipped build ever wrote a Variable without it, and the trigger is an out-of-band edit or file corruption.
criteria: C4 - silent data loss the user cannot detect or undo: one malformed nested object discards the entire custom-server list with no message (the try? at MCPStore.swift:247), and the first subsequent edit atomically overwrites mcp-customs.json with the empty list (MCPStore.swift:275). There is no backup, no undo, and nothing tells the user their file failed to parse.
triaged.notes: Escalated under the standing ruling: isolated, neither reproduced nor repaired, implementation deferred to the owner's decision. Recorded deliberately at the LOW end of consequential so the owner can dispose of it quickly - the trigger needs an out-of-band file edit, the symptom (an empty list) is immediately visible even though its cause is not, no credentials are destroyed, and the lost data is configuration the user can retype. It is escalated rather than reproduced only because the on-disk overwrite is irreversible from inside the app, which is what takes it out of 'no lasting harm'. This blocks nothing: the custom-MCP decode path can be left unimplemented or stubbed behind the decision while the rest of the MCP subsystem is specified and built. If the owner rules REPRODUCE, the port copies the synthesized-decoder throw and the whole-list try? exactly as upstream. Separate from UNK-0010 (entry 68), which is untouched here.

triaged.one_line: A token response without expires_in leaves no expires_at, accessToken then treats the session as never-expiring, and the proxy's 401 retry becomes a byte-identical replay that gets the same 401.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED verbatim, all three sites. MCPOAuth.swift:170-173 'let needsRefresh: Bool = { guard let expiresAt = json[expires_at]?.double else { return false }; return Date().timeIntervalSince1970 >= expiresAt - 90 }()' followed by :174 'guard needsRefresh else { return accessToken }' - no expires_at means never refresh. :699-701 'if let expiresIn { session[expires_at] = Date().timeIntervalSince1970 + Double(expiresIn) }' - expires_at is written only when the response carried expires_in (:633 and :672 both source it as json[expires_in]?.int). MCPProxy.swift:354-361 'if route.usesOAuth, http?.statusCode == 401 { if let refreshed = try? await MCPOAuth.accessToken(serverID: serverID) { request.setValue(Bearer refreshed, ...); (stream, response) = try await URLSession.shared.bytes(for: request); ... } }' - accessToken returns the same stored token, so the replayed request is identical. 'No forced refresh anywhere' checks out: performRefresh (:641) has exactly one caller, accessToken :180, reachable only through the needsRefresh gate.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: For an OAuth MCP server whose token endpoint omits expires_in, once the access token expires server-side every request through the proxy 401s, retries once identically, 401s again, and the client sees a bare 401. The server's tools stop working until the user signs in again from settings. Note the direction: this fails closed. No token is exposed, nothing is sent anywhere new, and the stored refresh token is untouched.
triaged.notes: I checked C2 and C3. No secret is leaked (the token only ever goes to the upstream the user chose, in an Authorization header) and no control is weakened (the upstream's rejection is honored; the app just cannot recover from it). Broken feature requiring a manual re-sign-in. Reproduce the conditional expires_at write, the 90-second skew and the single identical retry.

triaged.one_line: The failed set is read only by tools(); a server whose listTools threw is dropped from the tool list but relaunched on any direct call(), because call() never consults failed.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED. 'private var failed: Set<String> = []' at :48; 'if failed.contains(id) { continue }' at :59 inside tools(); 'failed.insert(id)' at :67-68 in the catch. In call() (:78-97) there is no reference to failed: the only early exit is :82-86 'if let cached = toolCache[parsed.server], !cached.contains(where: { $0.name == parsed.tool }) { throw MCPHubError.unknownTool(callName) }', and after a listTools failure no toolCache entry was ever written (:64 only runs on success), so that guard is skipped and :87 'let client = self.client(for: parsed.server, spec: spec)' relaunches the server.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: A server that failed to list its tools is re-spawned on every direct call, so a broken server can be restarted repeatedly within one run instead of staying quarantined. Reaching this needs a caller that names a tool of a server whose tools were never listed, which the model normally cannot do because those tools were absent from tools(). Realistic effect: repeated failed process spawns and repeated error messages. Nothing lost or written.
triaged.notes: Ineffective guard, mostly unreachable. Reproduce call() without the failed check.

triaged.one_line: initialized is cleared only by stop(), and the HTTP path has no restart or dead state, so an HTTP client whose remote session was dropped keeps believing it is initialized.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED. A grep for initialized in MCPHub.swift gives the declaration at :164, the single clear at :187 (inside stop(), alongside sessionID = nil at :188), the stdio guard at :313, the stdio set at :384, and the HTTP read/set at :425/:437. httpRPC (:421-452) does its initialize handshake only inside 'if !initialized' (:425-441) and has no path that resets the flag on any later failure - checkReply throwing at :448 propagates without touching it. So only stop() can un-stick it, and reload() (:99 onward) is what calls stop().
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: After a remote streamable-HTTP MCP server restarts or expires the session, every subsequent tool call from an API provider fails with the server's own session error until something triggers MCPHub.reload() - which MCPStore.exportAll does on connect, disconnect or enable/disable (MCPStore.swift:288-289). Until then the user sees repeated tool errors for that server. The failure is visible and self-explanatory in the error text; nothing is lost.
triaged.notes: Stale internal state producing loud, recoverable failures. Reproduce the single clear site in stop() and the absence of a re-init path in httpRPC.

triaged.one_line: SecItemUpdate's query carries no kSecAttrAccessible, so an item created by an earlier build keeps its original accessibility forever; only the SecItemAdd fallback applies kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED as a description of the code, with a correction to the implied risk. Source: set(_:server:field:) builds its query at :36-40 from kSecClass, kSecAttrService and kSecAttrAccount only, calls 'SecItemUpdate(query as CFDictionary, [kSecValueData as String: data] as CFDictionary)' at :41, and only the not-found fallback merges 'kSecAttrAccessible as String: kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked' at :44-48 before SecItemAdd at :49. So accessibility is indeed set on create and never on update. CORRECTION to the implication: there is no state in which this leaves a secret more exposed than intended. 'git log -p --follow' on the file shows exactly two commits (739518735 'Add MCP server support' and 75e30f217) and kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked is present on the add path in both - no shipped build ever created these items with a weaker accessibility, and the macOS default for an add without the attribute is kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked anyway. The 'never migrates' observation is therefore true and currently inert.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: Nothing observable. Every item this code can encounter was created with kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked, so there is no weaker setting for the update to preserve. The defect would only matter if a future build changed the desired accessibility, at which point existing items would not follow.
triaged.notes: I checked C2 and C3 deliberately, because this is a secret-storage path, and rejected both on the history evidence above: no secret is more exposed than intended in any reachable state. Port note, not a reproduction instruction: Windows has no kSecAttrAccessible equivalent - secrets go through DPAPI - so this attribute has no counterpart and the port must record that as an ENGINEERING DECISION rather than inventing an analogue.

triaged.one_line: randomToken fills bytes with UInt8.random(in:) rather than SecRandomCopyBytes for the PKCE verifier (32 bytes) and the CSRF state (24 bytes).
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED at source, and the lead's recorded correction is right and is upheld here. Source: :815-820 'private static func randomToken(byteCount: Int) -> String { var bytes = [UInt8](repeating: 0, count: byteCount); for index in bytes.indices { bytes[index] = UInt8.random(in: UInt8.min...UInt8.max) }; return base64url(Data(bytes)) }' (the body ends at :820, not :821). Call sites: :135 'let verifier = randomToken(byteCount: 32)' and :137 'let state = randomToken(byteCount: 24)'. base64url is :828 onward and the PKCE S256 challenge is :823-826. NOT an upstream weakness: UInt8.random(in:) with no explicit generator uses Swift's SystemRandomNumberGenerator, which is documented as cryptographically secure and is backed by the platform CSPRNG on Apple platforms. Upstream generates strong tokens.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: None upstream. The generated verifier and state are cryptographically strong. The risk lives entirely in the port: a Windows implementation that reads this entry as 'upstream used a plain RNG, so we can too' and reaches for a non-cryptographic generator would create a guessable PKCE verifier and CSRF state, which is an authorization-code-interception and CSRF exposure the original does not have.
triaged.notes: Not an upstream defect at all, so nothing to escalate. Reproduce exactly: byte counts 32 and 24, and the base64url encoding (standard base64 with plus mapped to hyphen and slash mapped to underscore), because those are parity-relevant. The random source is the port's own choice and MUST be a Windows CSPRNG (BCryptGenRandom or an equivalent that documents CSPRNG backing) - carried as an ENGINEERING DECISION in the adaptation register, not as behavior copied from the source. This matches the lead's existing correction at the foot of upstream_defects.md; I confirm it rather than re-opening it.

triaged.one_line: A missing url or command becomes the empty string in the emitted config rather than skipping the entry, so a malformed resolved server still produces a syntactically valid but unusable provider entry.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED verbatim at all eight cited lines. A grep for the empty-string coalescing in MCPProviderConfig.swift returns :10 url (claude remote), :18 command (claude stdio), :34 and :41 (codex remote and stdio), :59 and :66 (copilot remote and stdio), :131 httpUrl and :136 command. In each case the entry is still inserted into the emitted map; nothing skips a server on a nil field.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: A resolved server missing its url or command is written into the agent's MCP config with an empty value. The agent CLI then fails to start that one server - an empty command spawns nothing, an empty url is not a valid address - and reports it in its own startup output. The other servers in the same config are unaffected. Reaching this at all is hard: enabledServers only yields servers with a resolvable catalog entry, and saveCustom validates before writing (MCPStore.swift:165 via MCPCustomError.validate).
triaged.notes: I checked C3 (an empty string reaching a process launch) and C6 (an empty string reaching a network call). Neither holds: an empty command is not a command - it fails to resolve to any executable rather than resolving to an unintended one - and an empty url is not a valid destination. Reproduce all eight empty-string fallbacks exactly.

triaged.one_line: proxy-port is never deleted by anything, so a reinstall over an existing data folder reuses the previously chosen port - the collision the repick logic exists to paper over.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED verbatim. A tree-wide grep for proxy-port and portFile returns exactly four hits, all in MCPProxy.swift: the definition at :15 'private static let portFile = MCPPaths.directory.appendingPathComponent("proxy-port")', the read at :18 inside loadPort(), and the two writes at :23 (loadPort's first pick) and :31 (repickPort). No removeItem, no reset path, nothing in any uninstall or migration code touches it.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: A reinstall or a fresh install over a retained data folder starts on the port a previous install chose. If something else has taken it, the listener fails, the repick at MCPProxy.swift:126-127 moves to a new port, and entry 9's stale-config symptom follows for that launch. Worst case is one launch of unavailable MCP tools, self-correcting afterwards. No data loss.
triaged.notes: Stale persisted state with a bounded, recoverable effect. Reproduce the file's lifecycle exactly, including the absence of any delete, and keep the file name proxy-port.

triaged.one_line: Unconditional print() logging to stdout, not behind any debug flag, at five sites.
triaged.verified_against_source: CONFIRMED verbatim, and the set is exactly five. A grep for print( in MCPProxy.swift returns :105 'MCPProxy: could not listen on <port>', :117 'MCPProxy: listening on <port>', :119 'MCPProxy: listener on <port> failed: <error>', :313 'MCPProxy: request to <serverID> failed: <error.localizedDescription>' with the id in single quotes in the source; a grep in MCPHub.swift returns :67 'MCPHub: <id>: <error.localizedDescription>'. None is guarded by a flag. All five cited line numbers and all five message shapes match the register exactly.
triaged.worst_realistic_outcome: Noise on the app's stdout, which for a launched GUI app nobody normally reads. The interpolated values are a loopback port number, a server id, and an error's localizedDescription. I checked the last of these for secret exposure: tokens are carried in the Authorization header built at MCPProxy.swift:350 and never in a URL, and URLError/MCPHubError descriptions do not carry request headers, so no token or key can reach these lines.
triaged.notes: I checked C2 specifically because logging is a common leak path; it does not apply here, per the header-versus-URL analysis above. Reproduce all five messages with their exact prefixes, punctuation and interpolated values.

recorded_entries_found_wrong: Entry 2 (AntigravitySession dead mode fields): the dead-store fact is correct but the stated consequence is wrong and must not be propagated. The register says 'A mid-thread mode or Plan/Build change cannot reach agy at all, and even a relaunch uses the original modes while picking up the UPDATED model/effort'. CORRECTION: ThreadRuntime.swift:504-519 includes launchRuntimeMode and launchInteraction in SessionSignature, and :1414/:1418 populate both from thread.* for .antigravity, so the reuse check at :1422 fails on any mode or Plan/Build change and :1496-1523 constructs a brand-new AntigravitySession from a fresh SessionConfiguration carrying the CURRENT modes. AntigravitySession is constructed at exactly one site (ThreadRuntime.swift:1516) and start() is only ever called on a freshly made object, so the relaunch cannot carry stale modes. launchModel and launchEffort are in the signature too, so there is no 'half applied, half discarded' asymmetry. The true finding is a harmless pair of write-only properties. This matters for the port: the Antigravity entries in SessionSignature are what keep the --dangerously-skip-permissions gate honest, and dropping them would turn this harmless quirk into a real C3/C5 defect that upstream does not have.

Entry 21 (MCPKeychain accessibility never migrates): the description of the code is accurate, but the implied security weakness is not realizable and should not be propagated. CORRECTION: 'git log -p --follow DroppyCode/Services/MCP/MCPKeychain.swift' shows exactly two commits (739518735, 75e30f217) and kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked is present on the SecItemAdd path in both, so no shipped build ever created these items with a weaker accessibility for the update path to preserve; the macOS default for an add without the attribute is the same value in any case. The observation is true and currently inert. Recorded so the port does not carry it forward as a security finding - and noted that Windows has no kSecAttrAccessible analogue at all, since secrets go through DPAPI.

Entry 17 (custom-MCP decode drops every custom server): not wrong, but INCOMPLETE in a way that changes its classification. The register records only that every custom server is dropped silently. It does not record that the drop is followed by an overwrite: customs stays empty and the next saveCustom (MCPStore.swift:175) or deleteCustom (:196) calls saveCustoms, which atomically writes the empty array over mcp-customs.json (:275). That is what takes the defect out of 'no lasting harm' and into C4, and it is why this entry is escalated rather than reproduced. Two smaller citation corrections in the same entry: the tolerance doc comment is at MCPCustom.swift:36-37, not :37-38, and the outer try? is at MCPStore.swift:247, inside the :245-248 load block.
